mappings.note: The stem hands the student a case that looks like a broken law (open beaker, nothing left) and asks whether the law is violated. That is LO-49's own worked question, 'Are there any chemical changes that do not obey the law of conservation of mass?', almost verbatim. Not LO-48, which would be a bare statement of the law, and not LO-39's verification clause, because no apparatus is designed or operated here.

20 g + 160 g = 180 g is the conservation law used to predict a product mass, with no vessel, balance or observation in the stem. LO-40 owns the law in use; LO-48 is reserved here for items that only name or state it, and LO-39's clause needs measured bench data to verify against.

Constant proportions applied: 40:60 fixed to 2:3, so 20 g S demands 30 g O. LO-40 is the only outcome that names the law of constant proportions. Not LO-41, whose calculations are enumerated as ion charge, valency from atomic number, and molecular/formula unit mass - a combining mass ratio is not on that list.

Same demand as the sulfur/oxygen item: hold the 3:4 ratio fixed and scale it to 9 g of carbon. This numerical family honestly shares LO-40 with the other constant-proportions items; the frame offers no separate 'apply the law quantitatively' outcome to split them on.

Two halves: why the law holds for compounds (LO-40) and what a mixture is that makes it fail there. The mixture half is the only place C1.2's 'types and properties of mixtures' clause bites in this chapter, and it is what separates this item from the plain constant-proportions questions.

Two students' data, 4:1 and 8:2, must be reduced and compared to show the law survives. This is explaining the law through a test case, LO-40, not stating it (LO-48) and not a conservation-of-mass verification (LO-39).

The item turns entirely on a misquoted Dalton postulate - combination in whole-number ratios is by NUMBER of atoms, not by mass. LO-40 is the only outcome that names Dalton's atomic theory, so the discrimination lives there rather than in LO-48, whose particle clause is not what is being misstated.

Drawing N2 with three shared pairs is the 'formation of covalent compounds' clause of LO-40. Not LO-39: nothing is being differentiated from an ionic species; the whole answer is one bonding mechanism.

F2 formation from configuration 2,7. The atomic number is used only to reach the configuration, so LO-41's 'valency from the atomic number' is incidental; the graded demand is the sharing mechanism, which is LO-40.

Three molecules built by sharing, one of them with double bonds. Still the covalent-formation clause of LO-40; the item never asks how many electrons or what mass, so LO-41 and LO-42 have nothing to grade.

Neon is the negative case of the same outcome: a full octet means no transfer and no sharing, so no compound forms. LO-40's 'formation of ionic and covalent compounds' is what is probed, in the negative; nothing here is differentiated (LO-39) or calculated (LO-41).

Configuration 2,6 gives a 2- charge: this is LO-41's 'calculate the charge on an ion' and 'valency from the atomic number' clauses exactly. Not LO-40, because no compound is formed and no bond is explained.

The blanks are the chloride ion and the ion counts one and two - that is charge balancing, LO-41's ion-charge clause. Deliberately not LO-42: the item stops short of writing MgCl2, so no formula convention is exercised.

Show K and Ca losing electrons and combining with chlorine. The demand is the ionic formation mechanism (LO-40), not the charge arithmetic (LO-41) and not the written formula (LO-42), both of which fall out of the diagram rather than being asked for.

Na2S by two-for-one electron transfer - the ionic half of LO-40's formation clause. Sibling item d92dab9a shares this outcome honestly; both are 'illustrate the transfer', and the frame has no outcome that separates one-electron from two-electron donors.

Naming CO2, NO2, SF6, PCl3 exercises the prefix convention, which sits in LO-42's 'use scientific conventions' clause. It is the inverse of writing a formula, and the frame has no separate nomenclature outcome, so LO-42 carries both directions.
Name to formula, including the -ous/-ic stems (ferric, cuprous). This is LO-42's core clause, conventions and valency into a written formula. Not LO-41: no mass or charge is computed.
Fe(OH)3 and K2CO3 from given ion charges. The bracket around OH is the convention being graded, so LO-42; the charges are supplied rather than derived, which is what keeps this off LO-41.

A property profile - insulating solid, conducting solution - is used to name the bond type. That is LO-39's 'differentiate between chemical species based on their properties or characteristics ... ionic and covalent compounds'. Not LO-40: no formation mechanism is asked for, only a classification from evidence.

Three demands split across two outcomes: predicting the formula MO from a two-electron valency is LO-42, while the bond-type and conductivity parts are the property-based ionic/covalent discrimination of LO-39.

Straight sum of atomic masses for HNO3 - 'calculate ... the molecular mass' in LO-41's own words. Not LO-39, which would apply only if the item made the student choose between molecular mass and formula unit mass.

CH4 molecular mass. Identical demand to the HNO3 item and mapped identically on purpose: within LO-41 the frame draws no distinction between one covalent compound and another, and inventing one would be dishonest.

KCl formula unit mass. LO-41 names formula unit mass alongside molecular mass, so the ionic/covalent switch does not change the outcome; the item never asks why the term differs, which is what would pull in LO-39.
Mg(OH)2 formula unit mass, with the bracket multiplying through. The bracket is read, not written, so LO-42 is not engaged; the graded step is arithmetic, LO-41.

Six parts that fall cleanly in two: how many electrons given or taken and what charge results is LO-41's ion-charge/valency clause; the final formula for the compound is LO-42. The bond-type part follows from the charges rather than being explained, so LO-40 is not cited.
